UB PEP Uncrewed Team
The Furnas
University at Buffalo
Uncrewed Boat
Aiden Nabinger
Andrew Vickery
Davin Spier
Eric Sandle
Jacob DiFrancesco
Van Hywel ValenciaBackground

Much of what we needed to research surrounded our main design changes made between
last year’s unmanned boat team design and the current design. Thanks to our graduate advisor for
the project, Zack Medicis, many of our design changes and reasonings for each were made clear.
One being that we needed to change the hull type. Catamaran hulls are very stable and fast
however are not as fast as a v-shaped monohull. The tradeoff we found, was a decrease in
stability in harsh wake to an increase in overall thrust output. A v-shaped hull with steps on the
bottom of the hull, as seen in figure 3, acts as a platform for the boat to skim along while it is at
speed. The v-shape of the overall hull cuts through the water like a knife and the steps push the
boat upward and out of the water. When the boat is pushed out of the water more there is less
skin drag acting upon the boat from the water as air acts with less resistance with the water. And
researching a proper model v-shaped monohull to fabricate would be paramount for the specs of
the boat.
Much of the research for the internal layout and design of electronics was done by
consulting our advisor Zach and the previous boat. We pushed for not only one motor so
designing with Zach a proper electronic layout including how to integrate multiple safety
measures such as a fuse and a kill switch. The dual parallel systems for each set of batteries and
motors also needed to properly communicate with the receiver. Much of the research regarding
the receiver consulted the user manual for the receiver and remote control for the watercraft.
The inclusion of two motors meant that there would be two independent propellors acting
as thrusters for the craft. The interaction between these two propellors and how it would affect
the overall speed and steering of the craft came into question. How would we orient these
propellors? Would we need to make the dual propellors counter rotate to stop the hull from
turning with two propellors? One of our team members had an old Textbook regarding the
Principals of Naval Architecture, from the society of naval Architecture & Marine Engineers.
The book had these answers regarding the drivetrain and this new design change. As the dual
propellors would need to spin in opposite directions to stop the craft from slightly turning
whenever thrusting forward.
Our boat would need to be made from scratch, so our team would need to learn how to
properly produce layups of fiberglass and techniques that strengthen the material. With the help
of the University at Buffalo AIAA team and a student by the name of Thomas Przedwiecki we
got this completed. Thomas has had multiple previous experiences making fiberglass layups for
aerospace applications. Not only did he help us find and purchase the right materials, UB AIAA
was there to offer us resources to help produce the hull itself.
Later on in this report, we go over materials testing regarding the structural integrity of
the fiberglass hull. While fiberglass is strong for its weight, we were uncertain if the hull alone
with fiberglass would support the weight from the boat moving at speed. Conducting a tensile
test on samples of differing layers of fiberglass would help us visualize the strength of our hull. Design & Analysis

Electrical & Propulsion:
The speed of the boat can be theoretically calculated by looking at the KV value of the
motors, voltage through the system and the pitch of the propeller. The KV value of the two
motors is 540KV, the voltage though the system is 34V with a charge of 4.2V per cell, and a
pitch of 1.9 in/s for the propellers.
RPM is defined as:
𝑅𝑃𝑀 = 𝐾𝑉 × 𝑉
where RPM = revolutions per minute, KV = KV value of the motor, V = voltage.
Speed which will is defined as:
v = RPM × P × GR
where v = velocity, P = pitch, and GR = gear ratio.
Since we do not have a gear ratio incorporated into the system, we can assume that the gear ratio
is 1 and it would just simplify to RPM x GR. Inserting all the measured values, we can get a
speed of around 33mph.
Hull:
Many notices of concern were rightly brought up by members of the team and from TA
Karim about confirmation about the structural integrity of the hull. Mainly questioning if the
chosen number of layers for the fiberglass layup was the correct amount. We conducted a Tensile
test to determine the effect on tensile strength adding more layers of the fiberglass had. These tests
were applied to at least 5 samples of each type tested to follow ASTM guidelines for a Tensile test.
The samples were 4-layer, 6-layer, and 8-layer fiberglass layups, respectively. The results are
shown in Table 2.
Table 1: Major tensile test findings# layers

width)

Where σ = tensile strength, N = number of samples, µ = average, x = elemental value
Note that the calculated tensile strength [Equation]decreased for the increase of layers
between 6 and 8 layers. Also note that the 6-layer tensile strength was the largest. Our group's
hypothesis is that the decrease in tensile strength between 6-layers and 8-layers was due to the
increase in epoxy usage. As the layers between each epoxy layer grew, each layer of the weaving
of the fiberglass spread apart from one another. The interaction between each layer of fiberglass
is the main factor in strengthening the material. Having such a large tensile strength for our 6-
layer lay-up (19260.75±1439.31 lbs/in^2) assured our team that the boat would be structurally
sound. And that the main concern was any weakening of the boat from improper manufacturing
of the fiberglass layers. Such as excessive epoxy between layers, delamination, and bubbles.Overview of Build & Fabrication Processes

Hull:
Figure 1. Fabricated Hull
The top half of the hull consists of four layers of 0.2 mm fiberglass, and the bottom is six
layers. Our manufacturing process involved wet-laying the fiberglass over a 3D-CNC'd
foam mold with epoxy resin. The angle at which the threads of the fiberglass are directed
vary in 45° increments to increase the tensile strength in all directions. The resulting
product is exceptionally durable, lightweight, easy to manufacture, and cost-effective.
Table 2: Boat Specifications
Design Specifications Data Value
Fiberglass Sheet Thickness 0.2 mm
Layers in bottom hull 6
Layers in top hull 4
Width 18.91”
Length 71.8”
Bottom Hull Depth 5.69”
Top Hull Depth 3.24”
Hull Depth (combined) 8.93”
Depth Submerged with 60-lb payload 3.2”
Cost to Manufacture $262Figure 2. Modified CAD Model

This is the final CAD model of the hull in SolidWorks.
Figure 3. Original CAD Model
This is the original model for our hull. It originally had a hump on the top that was also
part of a removable lid, and it served mostly as a cosmetic design choice. Since the hump
created issues in neatly laying the fiberglass over the mold, it was removed in the final
design as shown above. This also allowed us to cut a door more easily into the top of
the hull. Note in Figure 3 there are small steps along the bottom of the hull from tip totail. These steps act as a floor for the water as the hull is pushed out of the water.

There are stringers that run down the length of the inside of the bottom boat hull section.
Since our hull mold was CNC’d with rigid polyurethane we decided to leave a small flat section
at the bottom of the hull to act as a floor. The foam is only about an inch deep towards the
surface of the fiberglass hull and is a minor factor towards the hull’s rigidity. The stringers were
adhered in place with 3M Marine Adhesive Sealant 5200 and JB weld. The Stringers were
modeled in SolidWorks and cut from a .188in thick sheet of aircraft aluminum with a waterjet
cutter. The stringers act to stabilize the hull and prevent the fiberglass from flexing inwards dur
to forces acting against the skin of the hull.
Figure 4: Bottom section of the hull showing alignment of aluminum stringers
Holes were drilled in the rear of the boat, and brass sleeves were glued down with epoxy
to act as guide holes for the drivetrain to feed through to the water. The mounts for the dual
electric motors were epoxied down along the sloped sides fiberglass besides the stringers. The
mounts were places such that the flex shafts reach through the brass guide holes.
Electrical & Propulsion:
The whole electrical system contains 8, 14.8V lithium 4 cell batteries, a kill switch, fuse,
telemetry sensor, 2 electronic speed controllers, 2 motors, servo and receiver. The system outputs
around 34V through the system if the batteries are held at a 4.2V per cell or if the batteries are
held at 3.8V the system can sustain a 31V power through the system. Each motor has a 540KV
rating which can get the propeller to spin at a range of 16,740-18360rpm depending on how
much voltage the cells are charged up to. The battery harness that connects all the batteries together are connected in series as well as parallel to allow the voltage to be below the 55V

maximum set by this competition. Most of the electronics are soldered together using 8-gauge
wire.
Figure 5: Electronical diagram of propulsion and telemetry system
Figure 6: Electrical system Fully wired up within bottom hull before constructionThe propulsion system uses 3/16” propellers and steps down from a ¼” shaft to the

propeller 3/16”. The propeller is secured onto the shaft via a drive dog to prevent it from sliding
while the shaft rotates and is held in place from the other end by a bullet nut for more fluid
dynamic movement to prevent as much cavitation as possible.
Risks
Design and Building
For the 2025 PEP Competition, the unmanned team from the University at Buffalo was
given a clear set of design changes from the previous year’s team. In the 2024 competition, the
University at Buffalo brought a roughly four-foot-long catamaran boat. This boat was submerged
nearly six feet by a wake that formed in front of it during the competition. This incident flooded
the internal components and shook the battery connections out of place. This failure significantly
affected the team’s performance and is to be avoided with the next iteration.
When meeting with the 2024 team, we were told how we could potentially solve this
issue in our design. From the list of possible design changes, our team chose to increase the hull
length, create a second motor system, and securing the batteries with brackets instead of Velcro
strips. The hull length increase is meant to solve the concern of wakes in the water, as the
increased length makes it harder to get the bow-end submerged. Having a second motor in
parallel with the original system will increase our speed, as well as reduce the risk of system
failure due to broken connections. The use of brackets will ensure that the batteries cannot move
within the boat under any circumstances, including capsizing. These three changes were outlined
as our design improvements at the start of the project.
Risk Mitigation
Operating an entirely electric boat involves several risks, most of which are electrocution
or electrical failure. The electrical system has been designed to split into two segments, both of
which are separate except for the safety and telemetry systems. As per the PEP Competition
Rules, the circuit must include a manual kill switch and a fuse. The kill switch has the entirety of
the batteries' current passing through it, and can be deactivated by twisting the handle and disconnecting the circuit. The kill switch is added in case a situation occurs where the boat will

not respond to inputs from the controller, or when the circuit is compromised and poses an
electrocution hazard. The fuse is after the kill switch in the circuit, and serves as an emergency
failsafe. If it is not safe or possible to disengage the kill switch, the fuse serves as a built-in
disconnect where the circuit will break. This is put in place to protect the speed controllers at the
end of the circuit, as they are sensitive to the total current passing through them.
